chunks.title: Peripheral retina anatomy
chunks.tldr: Ciliary body starts 1 mm behind limbus: pars plicata 2 mm + pars plana 4 mm. Enter at 4 mm phakic, 3.5 mm pseudophakic. Vitreous base (3–4 mm, straddles ora) = strongest attachment; holes inside it don't cause RD.
points: Ora serrata: retina meets ciliary body; retina–RPE fusion stops SRF at the ora. Choroid isn't stuck to sclera → choroidal detachments go past the ora.
Dentate processes (more nasal), oral bays, meridional folds (superonasal; may have a hole at apex), enclosed oral bays (don't mistake for holes).
Vitreous adhesion strength: base (very strong) > disc margin > fovea > peripheral vessels.
Blunt trauma can avulse the vitreous base.
chunks.hook: 4 for phakic, 3.5 for pseudo — the lens needs extra room.

cards.q: Strongest site of vitreoretinal adhesion?
Pars plana entry distance in phakic vs pseudophakic eyes?

chunks.title: Harmless degenerations & definitions
chunks.tldr: Harmless: microcystoid, paving stone, reticular (honeycomb), peripheral drusen, pars plana cysts. RRD = break + fluid >1 DD from break. Tractional = pulled, no break. Exudative = fluid from vessels.
points: Microcystoid: nearly all adults, near ora; can lead to degenerative retinoschisis.
Paving stone: yellow-white atrophic patches, inferior, ≥25% of eyes.
Reticular: perivascular pigment network. Pars plana cysts: 5–10%, temporal.
Risky adhesions: lattice, pigment clumps, cystic tufts, vitreous base anomalies, WWOP, zonular tufts.
Subclinical RD: asymptomatic, >1 DD from break but <2 DD behind equator.
Combined tractional–rhegmatogenous: break caused by nearby fibrovascular traction.
chunks.hook: Paving stones are safe to walk on.

cards.q: When is a break with SRF called a retinal detachment?
cards.a: When fluid extends more than one disc diameter from the edge of the break.

chunks.title: B-scan ultrasound basics
chunks.tldr: B-scan = 2D ultrasound for opaque media (dense vitreous haemorrhage). Marker up for vertical, to the nose for horizontal. Move probe opposite to gaze. High gain = weak echoes (vitreous); low gain = retina/sclera, sharper.
points: Gel/methylcellulose couples probe.
Marker shows at the left of screen.
Patient looks left (RE) → probe to right → nasal anterior fundus scanned.
Dynamic scans: patient moves eye, probe stays → judge mobility (RD mobile, TRD stiff).
chunks.hook: Gain = volume knob.

cards.q: Which gain setting best shows faint vitreous opacities?

chunks.title: Lattice & snailtrack degeneration
chunks.tldr: Lattice: 8% of people, in 40% of RDs, but lifetime RD risk only ~1%. Spindle-shaped thin areas with white sclerosed vessels, usually superotemporal, between equator and vitreous base. No prophylactic laser for asymptomatic lattice.
points: Commoner in moderate myopes; starts young.
Pathology: ILM gap, liquefied vitreous above, strong adhesion at margins.
Signs: white lattice lines, snowflakes, pigment, small holes.
RD routes: U-tear at edge after PVD, or atrophic holes in young myopes (slow, no PVD symptoms).
Snailtrack: frost-like bands of snowflakes; round holes, rarely U-tears; no prophylaxis.
Educate on RD symptoms + written info.
chunks.hook: Lattice = fence with weak edges — tears happen at the edge when vitreous pulls.

cards.q: Proportion of RDs with lattice degeneration?
Should asymptomatic lattice with holes be lasered?

chunks.title: Degenerative retinoschisis vs RD
chunks.tldr: Schisis: ~5% >20 yrs, hypermetropes, bilateral, inferotemporal. Smooth, thin, dome, immobile, absolute field defect, no flashes/floaters, no tobacco dust. Typical splits at OPL; reticular at NFL.
points: Grows from microcystoid degeneration.
RD = corrugated, opaque, mobile, relative field defect.
Inner layer breaks small/round; outer layer breaks large with rolled edges (behind equator).
Snowflakes, sclerosed vessels, bridging strands; telangiectasia (reticular).
Pigmented demarcation line → there's an RD too.
RD from schisis rare (~1% even with double-layer breaks), usually slow.
OCT distinguishes schisis from RD.
Observe; treat only if progressing to fovea or symptomatic RD.
chunks.hook: Schisis = Smooth, Still, Silent.

cards.q: Retinal layer split in typical degenerative retinoschisis?
Type of field defect in retinoschisis vs RD?
cards.a: Absolute in schisis; relative in RD.

chunks.title: Tufts, WWOP & myopic atrophy
chunks.tldr: Cystic retinal tuft: small white congenital lump with strong vitreous pull (5% of people; causes 5–10% of RDs). Zonular traction tuft: nasal, ~2% tear risk. WWOP: strong vitreous adhesion; giant tears can form at its edge.
points: CRT: glial tissue, temporal; holes and U-tears possible; per-eye risk <1%.
WWP: white with indentation; common, probably not risky.
WWOP in fellow eye of a giant retinal tear → consider prophylaxis.
Myopic chorioretinal atrophy: small holes hard to see (low contrast).
chunks.hook: WWOP + giant tear in other eye → treat.

cards.q: When is prophylaxis for white-without-pressure considered?
cards.a: When the fellow eye has had a spontaneous giant retinal tear.

chunks.title: Posterior vitreous detachment
chunks.tldr: Vitreous liquefies (synchysis) and collapses (syneresis), peeling off the retina. <10% under 50, ⅔ over 70. ~10% of acute PVDs have a tear; with vitreous haemorrhage ~60%. Tobacco dust (Shafer) → break likely.
points: Triggers: cataract surgery, trauma, uveitis, PRP.
Order: perifoveal → fovea → posterior retina → disc → up to vitreous base.
Symptoms: temporal lightning arcs with eye movement (dim light), floaters, Weiss ring, haze if blood.
Signs: crumpled membrane at slit lamp; blood; pigment ('tobacco dust') up to 95% sensitive for a break.
See within 24–48 h (sooner if myopia, RD history, Stickler, pseudophakia, field loss).
Examine 360° to ora with indentation; always check fellow eye.
Dense haemorrhage hiding fundus: 60–90% break, 40% RD → serial B-scan, low threshold for vitrectomy.
chunks.hook: Tobacco in the vitreous = smoke means fire (a tear).

cards.q: Chance of a retinal tear in acute PVD with vitreous haemorrhage?
What is the Shafer sign?
cards.a: Pigment cells ('tobacco dust') in the anterior vitreous – suggests a retinal break.

chunks.title: Types of retinal break
chunks.tldr: U-tear (flap still pulled = dangerous), operculated (flap torn free = safer), round hole (atrophic, young myopes, slow RD), dialysis (at ora, trauma, vitreous on posterior edge), giant tear (≥90°, vitreous on anterior edge).
points: ~1 in 5 symptomatic PVDs have a break; 8% of people have asymptomatic breaks.
PVD tears usually superotemporal; up to 5% appear weeks later.
Macular breaks from PVD: rare, round, myopes.
Dialysis: young man, blunt trauma, slow RD, rolled regular edge.
Giant tear: just behind ora; Stickler, myopia.
chunks.hook: Dialysis = vitreous holds the Back edge. Giant tear = holds the Front edge.

cards.q: Definition of a giant retinal tear?
cards.a: A tear involving 90° (3 clock hours) or more of the circumference.

cards.q: Usual cause of a retinal dialysis?

chunks.title: Which breaks to treat
chunks.tldr: Acute symptomatic U-tear → treat urgently (90% RD risk → 5%). Traumatic breaks/acute dialysis → treat. Asymptomatic U-tear, operculated tear, flat round holes → usually observe.
points: Risk ↑: fellow eye RD, cataract surgery (esp. vitreous loss), myopia, family history, Marfan/Stickler/Ehlers–Danlos.
Higher risk: symptomatic, large, persistent traction, U-shape, superior (gravity), equatorial, aphakia. Pigment around = chronic, stable.
Consider prophylaxis before cataract surgery, YAG capsulotomy, injections if risk factors.
Operculated: review 2–4 wks, 1–3 m, 6–12 m, yearly; treat if bridging vessel.
Asymptomatic U-tear: ~5% risk → observe.
Subclinical RD: ~10% symptomatic in 2–3 yrs → case by case.
Asymptomatic round holes: no treatment; review 1–2 yearly.
chunks.hook: Flashing + flap = laser today.

cards.q: RD risk of an untreated acute symptomatic U-tear?
Why are superior breaks riskier?
cards.a: Gravity drives fluid through them; superotemporal threatens the macula early.

chunks.title: Laser vs cryo retinopexy
chunks.tldr: Laser preferred (precise, less ERM). Cryo for very peripheral lesions, hazy media, small pupils, multiple tears. Laser: 2–3 rows of confluent burns. Cryo: −85 °C, single row, don't pull off till thawed.
points: Laser slit lamp: 0.1 s, 200–300 µm (3-mirror) or 100–200 µm (wide-field), start 200 mW → moderate blanching.
BIO laser: adjust spot with 20 D lens position.
Watch landmarks — don't burn the macula.
Cryo: purge probe, test (5 mm ice ball in water), indent under BIO until retina whitens, thaw 2–3 s.
After: no strenuous activity ~1 week; review 1–2 weeks.
chunks.hook: Laser = Little, precise. Cryo = Cold, for the far edge.

cards.q: Why is laser generally preferred to cryotherapy?
cards.a: More precise, less collateral damage, lower ERM risk.

cards.q: Cryotherapy temperature for retinopexy?

chunks.title: RRD: who gets it & finding the break
chunks.tldr: ~1:10,000/yr; 10% bilateral; >40% myopic. Breaks: 60% superotemporal; 50% have >1 break. Use Lincoff's rules: fluid shape points to the break.
points: Needs break + liquefied vitreous + traction.
Distribution: ST 60%, SN 15%, IT 15%, IN 10%.
Shallow inferior RD, higher on one side → inferior break on that side.
Inferior RD with equal levels → break at 6 o'clock.
Bullous inferior RD → break above horizontal.
Superonasal break → fluid wraps round disc and rises temporally.
Subtotal RD with superior wedge attached → break near highest border.
Fluid crossing midline above → break near 12; lower edge is on the break's side.
chunks.hook: Fluid falls, then climbs the other side — trace it back uphill to the break.

cards.q: Most common quadrant for the primary break in RRD?
Bullous inferior RD – where is the break?

chunks.title: RRD: symptoms & signs
chunks.tldr: Flashes + floaters (60%) → curtain field defect (break in opposite quadrant). Fresh RD: convex, corrugated, mobile, fluid to ora. Old RD: thin retina, intraretinal cysts (~1 yr), demarcation lines (~3 m).
points: Field loss may vanish in the morning (fluid absorbs overnight).
Location of flashes doesn't help localise the break.
RAPD if extensive; IOP ~5 mmHg lower; very low → choroidal detachment too.
Schwartz–Matsuo: RRD (often dialysis in young man) + 'uveitis' cells (photoreceptor outer segments) + high IOP; fixes after repair.
Tobacco dust, vitreous blood.
Breaks red; hard to see in pale myopic fundus.
Macular pseudohole when posterior pole detached.
B-scan: mobile retina and vitreous.
chunks.hook: Fresh = wrinkly and wobbly. Old = thin, cysts, tide marks.

cards.q: What is Schwartz–Matsuo syndrome?
cards.a: RRD with raised IOP and aqueous 'cells' (photoreceptor outer segments), often from a traumatic dialysis; resolves after repair.

cards.q: How long do demarcation lines take to develop?

chunks.title: Proliferative vitreoretinopathy (PVR)
chunks.tldr: Membranes on/under retina contract → stiff fixed folds. Grade A haze/pigment, B wrinkling + rolled break edges, C full-thickness star folds (anterior/posterior, clock hours). Commonest cause of late surgical failure.
points: Usually after RD surgery or penetrating injury; can occur primarily.
Reduced retinal mobility on eye movement/indentation.
Advanced: funnel-shaped retina.
Surgery: vitrectomy + membrane peel ± relieving retinotomy, silicone oil.
chunks.hook: A=Ash (haze), B=Bumpy (wrinkles), C=Crumpled stars.

cards.q: Hallmark of grade C PVR?

chunks.title: Choroidal detachment & uveal effusion
chunks.tldr: Choroidal detachment: brown, smooth, lobed domes, low IOP, extend past the ora, stop at vortex veins; may 'kiss'. No flashes/floaters. Uveal effusion syndrome: hyperopic middle-aged men/nanophthalmos → ciliochoroidal + exudative RD → leopard spots.
points: Causes: hypotony (post-trab), sulfonamides (acetazolamide, topiramate), uveitis, scleritis, tumours, cyclodialysis cleft.
Shallow AC → non-pupillary block angle closure.
Rx: treat cause; sometimes drainage via sclerotomy.
Uveal effusion: thick abnormal sclera → poor drainage; DDx ring melanoma, choroidal haemorrhage; Rx full-thickness sclerectomies.
chunks.hook: Choroidal = Chocolate-brown, low pressure, goes past the ora.

cards.q: Why don't choroidal detachments reach the posterior pole?
cards.a: They are limited by the vortex veins entering the sclera.

cards.q: Residual sign after uveal effusion syndrome?

chunks.title: RD surgery: urgency, pneumatic & buckle
chunks.tldr: Macula-on RD = urgent. Pneumatic retinopexy: gas + cryo/laser for small superior breaks (<2 clock hours, upper ⅔). Scleral buckle: indent sclera to close break + ease traction; always for dialysis.
points: Urgency ↑: macula on, superior/large break, myopic syneresis, dense VH with RD on B-scan. Nil by mouth.
Posture head so break is dependent.
Pneumatic gases: SF6, C3F8. Quick, office-based; lower success than buckle.
Buckle ~2 mm margin around break, include vitreous base anteriorly. Radial, segmental, circumferential, encircling.
Technique: peritomy → localise → cryo → suture explant → check.
SRF drainage (D-ACE) — risks: perforation, incarceration, choroidal haemorrhage.
chunks.hook: Macula on → operate on. Dialysis → buckle.

cards.q: Which RD should always be repaired with a scleral buckle?
Suitable case for pneumatic retinopexy?
cards.a: Uncomplicated RD with a small break (<2 clock hours) in the upper two-thirds.

chunks.title: Buckle complications & surgical failure
chunks.tldr: Buckle problems: diplopia, CMO (25%), ERM (15%), anterior segment ischaemia (encircling, sickle), extrusion/infection, IOP rise, choroidal detachment. Failure: PVR, missed breaks, new breaks; 'fish-mouthing'.
points: Diplopia usually settles.
Extrusion/infection → remove buckle + antibiotics.
Buckle failure: wrong size/position/height.
Fish-mouthing: big superior U-tear gapes open after buckling.
Reopening: inadequate cryo/buckle or buckle loses height.
PVR = commonest late failure (weeks later).
chunks.hook: Failed RD surgery = 'PMN': PVR, Missed breaks, New breaks.

cards.q: Three commonest causes of failed RD surgery?
cards.a: PVR, failure to close all breaks (missed breaks), new breaks.

cards.q: Buckle complication linked to sickle disease?

chunks.title: Tractional RD
chunks.tldr: Causes: PDR, ROP, penetrating trauma. Concave, immobile, no breaks, shallow, doesn't reach ora; highest where membranes pull. No flashes/floaters. Break appears → combined RD → spreads fast.
points: Diabetic PVD is slow/incomplete; vitreous stuck to NV.
Traction types: tangential, anteroposterior, bridging (trampoline).
Complete PVD in diabetes avulses NV → no TRD.
B-scan: incomplete PVD, stiff retina.
Vitrectomy if macula threatened (with anti-VEGF/endolaser); combined TRD-RRD urgently.
chunks.hook: Tractional = tent pulled up (concave). Rhegmatogenous = balloon (convex).

cards.q: Shape of a tractional RD?

chunks.title: Exudative RD
chunks.tldr: Fluid without break or traction. Smooth, convex, very mobile — shifting fluid. Tumour until proven otherwise. Others: Harada, posterior scleritis, bullous CSR, CNV, toxaemia, uveal effusion.
points: RPE pump overwhelmed → SRF.
No photopsia; floaters only if vitritis; field loss sudden.
Shifting: upright fluid inferior; supine → moves posteriorly.
Iatrogenic: RD surgery, PRP.
After flattening: leopard spots.
Rx cause: steroids for Harada/scleritis; laser for bullous CSR leak.
chunks.hook: Shifting fluid = look for a tumour.

cards.q: Hallmark sign of exudative RD?
Cause to exclude first in exudative RD?

chunks.title: Vitrectomy kit & tamponades
chunks.tldr: Small-gauge (23/25/27G) sutureless now standard. Gases: SF6 2× volume ~2 wk, C2F6 3× ~1 month, C3F8 4× ~2 months. No flying / nitrous oxide with gas. Silicone oil floats; heavy liquid (PFCL) sinks.
points: Cutter up to 5000–7500 cuts/min → less traction.
Chandelier light → bimanual surgery; wide-angle viewing systems.
Non-expansile mixes: SF6 20–30%, C3F8 12–16%.
Silicone oil 1000 cs (easier) vs 5000 cs (less emulsification) — PVR, long tamponade.
Perfluoro-n-octane: flattens posterior retina, floats dropped lens/IOL, controls bleeding; must be removed (toxic).

cards.q: Expansion and duration of C3F8?
Why avoid nitrous oxide anaesthesia after gas tamponade?
cards.a: N2O diffuses into the bubble, expanding it and raising IOP (risk of CRAO).

chunks.title: Vitrectomy: indications & technique
chunks.tldr: >80% of primary RD repair now PPV. Indications: breaks not visible, giant/posterior breaks, PVR, pseudophakic RD, macula-threatening TRD, combined TRD-RRD, trauma. Steps: infusion → remove gel + hyaloid → peel membranes → close breaks.
points: Ports: infusion inferotemporal (at lateral rectus lower border), others at 10 and 2 o'clock.
Stains: trypan blue for ERM, triamcinolone for vitreous.
Diabetic membranes: delamination (cut pegs horizontally), segmentation (vertical cuts), en-bloc.
PVR: peel membranes, scissors between folds, relieving retinotomy.
Trauma membranes are anterior (pre-equatorial/ciliary body).
chunks.hook: Diabetic membranes: Delaminate, Segment, or take En bloc ('DSE').

cards.q: What is delamination in diabetic vitrectomy?
cards.a: Horizontal cutting of vascular pegs to remove fibrovascular membrane from the retinal surface.

cards.q: Dye used to stain ERM during vitrectomy?

chunks.title: Vitrectomy complications
chunks.tldr: Breaks/RD, retinal fold, inflammation, raised IOP (gas over-expansion → tap with 30G needle; silicone pupil block → inferior Ando iridectomy; emulsified oil late), cataract (nuclear sclerosis, almost all with oil), band keratopathy.
points: Intraop: posterior/peripheral breaks, rarely choroidal haemorrhage.
Gas: transient feathery PSC.
Late silicone glaucoma: emulsified oil in angle → early removal; may need tube.
Others: ghost cell, steroid, inflammatory, ciliochoroidal effusion angle closure.
Post-vitrectomy nuclear cataract common, esp. >50 yrs.
chunks.hook: Oil floats up → blocks pupil in aphakes → inferior (Ando) iridectomy.

cards.q: Where is the Ando iridectomy placed and why?
cards.a: Inferiorly – silicone oil floats up, so aqueous can pass below it, preventing pupil block.

cards.q: Cataract after vitrectomy: typical type?
cards.a: Nuclear sclerosis (gas → transient posterior subcapsular feathering).
